Since it's been so many years since I last played OG Resident Evil 1, I forgot how much easier it is compared to the 2002 RE Remake. For example: just 15 minutes or so into OG RE1, I've found several pistol clips (totaling about 45-50 bullets), and you'll regularly see green herbs scattered around the map. The RE Remake, by comparison, is extremely stingy with giving you resources. It's far less common to find ammo and healing supplies around the maps. 

The further you get into this game, the more ammo and healing supplies you'll find. By the time I reached the labs, I was swimming in pistol, shotgun, and bazooka/grenade launcher ammo. And I had dozens of healing items stored in the item box, along with even more ammo (I had found so much ammo up to that point in the game that I couldn't even carry it all with me).

You get enough ammo in this game to kill every zombie, dog, and hunter you'll encounter throughout the game. You're handed so much resources, in fact, that the game actually loses a lot of the 'survival horror' feeling to the gameplay. 

This isn't a complaint. It's just an observation. And an inevitable comparison to the 2002 remake, which in my opinion delivers the full, quintessential 'survival horror' experience. 

I actually had a really good time playing through this a few times. Even though it's much easier than the Remake and has less content, this OG version feels like a much 'tighter' and more focused experience. The pacing is much faster. The game feels much shorter. But for repeated playthroughs - OR if you're binging the entire franchise, so you want to get through each game quickly - the tighter pacing and reduced difficulty feels nice.

I really tried to give the original Resident Evil (1996 video game) a fair shot, but I found it more frustrating than fun.

The biggest issue for me is the ammo balance. It’s not just “survival horror scarcity”—it feels excessive. There are too many enemies for how little ammo you’re given early on, which creates a constant sense of being underprepared no matter how carefully you play. Instead of building tension, it often turns into trial-and-error and backtracking.

I understand the argument that you’re supposed to avoid enemies, but in practice that doesn’t always work well. The tank controls and fixed camera angles make dodging feel unreliable and awkward. And when the alternative is relying on the knife—which feels weak and unsatisfying—the gameplay starts to feel clunky rather than tense.

I can respect how influential this game was in shaping the survival horror genre, but being important historically doesn’t automatically make it enjoyable to play today. Compared to later versions like the Resident Evil (2002 remake), parts of the experience feel outdated in ways that hurt the overall gameplay.

If you have nostalgia for it or enjoy very punishing resource management, you might still like it. Otherwise, this is one of those classics that may not click with everyone today.

Since I'm a big fan of the Resident Evil franchise, when this game was released here on Steam, I decided to give it a try. I've only played Jill's campaign so far, but I'm quite surprised at how well this game holds up to this day, and how ahead of its time this game must've been back in 1996!

Resident Evil 1 is survival horror at it's core, not only because of the claustrophobic rooms and narrow hallways, but also because of the inventory with limited slots, and the scarce resources that the game gives you. Frequently, I was undecided about whether I should use my ammo to clear a room, or spare them and risk being bitten by a zombie and waste an herb, for example. 
Also, the Spencer's mansion is such a unique scenario, and the soundtrack is terrifying and unnerving. The puzzles are challenging, and yet they're very fun to solve. The backtracking was so organic that I was always curious about what new doors I could open with a new key. It's noticeable how the developers thought of everything to give you the best survival horror experience back then. 
The story is very intriguing and has a few plot twists along the way, which is surprising for the year that it was released, despite the "iconic" voice-acting. 
Also, read the files for a better understanding of the story and the puzzles!

Overall, if you don't mind the tank-style controllers, I'm sure you'll have a blast playing this!

This is where it all began. As I never had the opportunity to play this game on any console at the time, my first experience with the series was through the Resident Evil HD Remaster, which I found to be one of the greatest survival horror games of all time. Now, having finally played the original 1996 version, I can confidently say that this game was far ahead of its time. The voice acting features some unintentionally humorous moments, which add a certain charm to the experience. The graphics are, understandably, dated and rough by modern standards, but the atmosphere remains strong. The background music is excellent and greatly enhances the overall tension and immersion. RE1 is an iconic game. It gave birth to an iconic franchise, which has seen many ups and many downs. Unfortunately, I wasn't even close to being alive when it first got released, so I can't even begin to imagine what it would have felt like to play it for the first time in the 90s. I can however, talk about how it felt like to play it for the first time in 2026. It felt special. The graphics were incredibly outdated, the voice acting was laughably bad, and the gameplay was very outdated, basic and clunky. But that's what made it so special to me. It made me feel like I time travelled back in history, into an era where perhaps, everything was better. I've played 90s games before, this isn't my first time playing a game that got released way before I was born, but there are only two games that have made me feel such a way, the other one being the original Half-Life. It truly is a special feeling, and the unbelievable atmosphere that these old games have is mostly to blame. Apart from the said feeling, however, there is no other reason to buy the original RE1. The RE1 Remake not only massively improves every single thing from the original, but builds upon it too, by adding many new areas, puzzles and twists. That being said, the choice is yours. If you wish to experience RE1, the Remake is by far the superior version. If you wish to experience the original specifically, then you are in for quite the experience. However, I do recommend playing both versions, as they are fundamentally different games and offer very different experiences.

This is essentially the GOG version of the original Resident Evil (1996), but with DRM added on top thanks to "Crapcom"

The game itself is great and runs well thanks to the improvements originally done for the GOG release—modern compatibility, rendering options, and overall stability. However, the Steam version adds Enigma DRM, which brings some downsides. You’re required to run it through Steam, and there have been reports of performance issues, glitches, and minor compatibility problems that don’t exist in the DRM-free version.

The biggest issue is that there’s no real benefit here compared to GOG. You’re getting the same game, but with restrictions added. No extra features, no improvements—just DRM layered over an otherwise solid port but with DRM that means NO MODS.

If you just want the game in your Steam library and can get it very cheap, it’s fine. But if you care about ownership, long-term usability, or avoiding unnecessary DRM, the GOG version is the better choice.

Muito obrigado Capcom por finalmente colocar essa trilogia original de Resident Evil na Steam, segunda vez que estou comprando e com muito gosto. Resident Evil para sempre será minha franquia favorita de jogos, ainda que repleta de erros e decaídas, mas quem ama esta do lado desde o início durante todos os seus passos e aqui estou eu, anos mais tarde depois de conhecer a franquia lá em 2001 com Resident Evil 3 de 1999, me apaixonando, caminhando junto a essa franquia por 25 anos da minha vida e ela em si tendo 30 anos.

Sou extremamente grato pelas experiências que a franquia me propôs e, como não poderia deixar de fazer, aqui está uma review do meu jogo favorito da franquia em sua era clássica. Existe algo especial em relação ao Game Design desse jogo que me faz ama-lo muito mais do que tudo que a franquia vai fazer até o lançamento de Resident Evil 4. O Level Design é incrível, magnífico, é de uma genialidade inexplicável o quão interconectado todos os lugares do jogo estão, o nível de labirinto que é a sensação de explorar eles mas o quão recompensador é, acima de tudo, conseguir desbloquear atalhos e voltar para lugares que estivemos antes e ver nosso progresso acontecendo diante dos nossos olhos.

Um combate satisfatório, balanceado o bastante para um primeiro jogo. Ainda mais um primeiro jogo que ousou tanto para sua época, fez tantas coisas inovadoras e hoje em dia, felizmente, é reconhecido devidamente pelo tanto de coisa que criou e estabeleceu na mídia dos videogames.

A História é uma porcaria? Sim.
A Dublagem é horrível? Sem sombra de dúvidas (mas acho que foi por conta de falta de direção e não tanto pelos atores). Mas existe uma certa magia em você experienciar esse jogo, ainda mais quanto mais o tempo passa e ver o quanto que ele ainda se sustenta tranquilamente. Meu Resident Evil favorito, de toda a série, sempre será Resident Evil 4 - em especial o Remake, anos depois, que assumiu o lugar do original. Controles modernos fizeram bem para a série, mas preciso dizer: Controle Tank? Ainda é tranquilo de se adaptar.

Não quero nem um pouco a volta deles, vai me parecer um regresso na evolução do combate e exploração da série. Mas se voltar? A memória muscular esta devidamente em dia, foi assustador o quão rapido eu consegui me ver dentro do universo do jogo novamente. Movimentação, Esquiva, Domínio com a Faca, Espaçamento... Olha, que jogo gostoso!

Bons tempos.
Bom jogo.
Boa franquia.
Bom porte.

Aliás, é isso que isso aqui é, viu, leitores.
Apenas um porte. E é o que ele deve ser.
Sem Upscaling. Sem nada além disso. Ele é um porte, portanto, jogue-o como um porte.

I would recommend playing this game with the Classic Rebirth patch. It fixes up some stuff and makes the game generally more compatible. Here are some quick instructions on how to do this, because there is some conflicting info online.

- Download the Classic Rebirth DLL itself from their website, along with the official 1.01 patch. Both should be on their website.
- Open your steam installation folder for the game (4249100_Biohazard in steamapps/common) and open the "japanese" folder. Copy the DLL in here.
- Cut all the contents of the japanese folder and paste them in the main folder.
- Replace Biohazard.exe with the official 1.01 patch. 
- Rename 4249100_Launcher.exe to something else, then rename your new Biohazard.exe to 4249100_Launcher.exe, effectively replacing it. This is the file Steam launches when you start playing the game through Steam, so this allows you to launch the Classic Rebirth version through Steam as normal.

Believe me, I've played this game a dozen times already, so just ignore the short playtime ([i]for now[/i]). 

When the original RE Trilogy launched on 04.02, of course I had to do a quick test run, which ended up being a little over 50 minutes with Jill. That alone should tell you how many times I've played RE1 ([i]to death[/i]).

This Steam release of the original Resident Evil offers a decent enough way to live through a near-perfect vanilla experience—the feeling how most people remember it from the PlayStation 1 days.

Not to say there aren't some sensible changes that were made to the original PC port that are retained here as well: you can still skip door opening sequences, and thanks to auto-aim, firing from a hip won't be a problem here. Beating the game without any saves will still grant you an Uzi for Jill and a Minimi for Chris—weapons that are exclusive to the PC version to this very day.

The inclusion of the Enigma DRM is an unfortunate pick, and while it doesn't hinder performance whatsoever, which would be crazy for a 30-year-old game, maybe with some pushback, Capcom could change their minds, like how they did with the RE4 Remake.

In the end, a solid version all around, I had no hiccups whatsoever. I'm pretty sure you can inject the GOG executables; Gemini's Classic Rebirth patch should work like a charm, and with that you can play all your favorite mods: BioRand, the GBC conversion, Real Survivor, etc.

Not to mention all the enhancements that Gemini's patch offers, such as a 180 quick turn, higher resolution, speed-up and so on.

If you want to go full vanilla, then go with Duckstation. If you want the best overall experience, go with this ([i]patched[/i]) or Deadly Silence on the Nintendo DS - that version also mapped the knife to the L button, which made such tool a lot more useful than before. And you could skip MOST cutscenes!

The game at the core of this experience is Resident Evil and is therefore good, it's got fantastic environment and puzzle design, and as a fan of the series going back to the very first game was interesting. I played through Jill's campaign in about 6 hours and enjoyed myself very much. 

I played through this with my PS5 controller connected via bluetooth and using Steam Input as an intermediary layer, which seemed to work well, though I've read that some other reviews which say the native controller support is terrible. I can't corroborate that, but the keyboard mapping is certainly non-obvious.

The larger problems with this version of the game are really weird, there's no pause menu or quit option, you just have to alt+f4 the game to quit out after you've saved, which I wouldn't mind from a free/open source/community made port, each of those comes with a degree of expected jank, but for any amount of money on the table and officially from Capcom I'd expect the bare minimum of quality of life features added. 

Worse still is that there's now DRM on a 30 year old game that costs £5. The DRM and launcher are weird and request registry access which I'm not happy about at all, and as a result of that don't work on the Steam Deck. I presume that means they don't work on linux at all, but I only tested them on the steam deck and couldn't get past the launcher, which I'm certainly disappointed about. 

With the DRM removed and a proper pause menu with graphics & sound options & quit button (for the entire trilogy to be clear) I'll gladly make this a positive review, but what a confoundingly stupid choice for Capcom to make when rereleasing these games. If you have a switch, I'd probably give the switch versions of the trilogy a go for the flexibility offered, though I admit I've not played those myself, and if you're a PC person, my understanding is that GOG has them DRM free. (also emulation is free, just saying)

I own all of these games physically on ps1 and play them at least annually since I very heavily enjoy them. I have played both the original release and Director's cut extensively, So I was very excited to finally have a digital version of these games as well. For this review, I did both a complete Jill and Chris run. Unfortunately, I do think this port is rather underbaked in several ways. 

Firstly, the game is WAY easier than the ps1 release for whatever reason. It felt like enemies did way less damage, and the first playthrough for Jill had removed ink ribbons entirely. Apparently this was how the original pc port came so it is just replicating that, but it caught me off guard. There is no steam support or overlay in game. The settings are barebones and very minimum especially for the modern year. And I don't expect much to be added to this 30 year old game, but I feel achievements wasn't too big of an ask for a $10 rerelease. Also, I'm not normally a guy who cares or complains about DRM, but why the hell would capcom put DRM in this? This game is 30 years old and has been emulated to death. You can download it for free on a ROM site and run it through duckstation. Who the hell is going to pirate the steam version?

To conclude with some positives, the original uncensored intro cutscene is fully restored with full color and gore. It was my first time actually seeing it in game. The textures do look better than the original release, to where you can make out details on the character models face.  I noticed that zombie limbs other than the head could come off with gunshots, which I don't think happens in the original release. These are the only credits I can give the game. Overall, I am happy to have this in my library, but I don't think i prefer it over my physical copies. Would not recommend to anyone unless they have no means to own physicals and are interested in playing the game. Especially not for ten dollars.

💾Graphics - This is a super old game, so the visuals are not gonna hold well at all. The backgrounds are really pixelated and the details are kinda hard to see at times, plus the resolution is pretty limited in the settings. Now I did install the RE:Enhanced mod, and that changed everything. Some quality of life improvements, and the most important thing, a massive graphical overhaul. This mod makes all the background look sharp and fresh, as well as the UI too and cutscenes. This gives the game a proper remastered look to it. In my opinion, this is how you should play the game. It’s extremely simple to install too. I’ll link the mod here: https://www.moddb.com/mods/reenhance-re1. This mod made my experience enjoyable and totally worth the download. If you are having issues with your controller and keyboard not working after booting up the game with the mod installed, simply restart your computer and it should work fine.

🎮Gameplay - This is classic survival horror! The movement here is actually super easy. Now maybe it’s because I played older games and gotten used to it, but I believe they made the controls easy to navigate with. It may take a little time for newcomers to the so-called “tank controls”, but believe me it’s not as intimidating as some may put it out to be. You have two characters you play as, Both Chris and Jill. Now playing as Jill is probably the best option for new players. Your first playthrough won’t require ink ribbons to save, and you have more inventory slots and the amazing lockpick. Chris on the other hand is the opposite, less inventory slots, and more locked doors. Roaming around the mansion and solving puzzles is the main challenge in this game basically. You can get lost on your first and second playthrough, as I have. The enemies for the most part, are extremely easy and don’t really offer much of a challenge. Now the hunters are the main challenge as well as the Tyrant of course. If you are good at conserving ammo and healing items and using the right weapons, this game is a cake walk. You do have a decent amount of weapons and healing items in your disposal. Just make sure to use them strategically and not waste them, like healing yourself over minor damage or trying to kill every enemy in the game. Just mainly target enemies in locations where you are trapped, or in locations you will be traveling through a lot. Also some enemies are weaker to certain weapons and ammo. The more you play, the more you will get better and understand the mechanics more. You should check out some guides beforehand. I will actually link a strategy guide below for you to check out. As for unlockables, you do have some secret costumes and weapons to unlock through beating the game in a certain time and certain endings. I will link a guide down below.

📜Story - The story in super basic. You and your team explore a crash site from one of your teams and you get ambushed by wild dogs. This chase leads you to the Spencer Mansion. This place will test your skills as you try and crack the clues to what has happened in this mysterious place. The further you go, more secrets will be unraveled. I don’t want to spoil the events and bosses, but the experience was fun and I did enjoy the story, even if it was pretty shallow. I did really enjoy the journal entries, as it told the true dark secrets and scary moments some of the residents had to endure.

🕛Playtime - My first playthrough was a little over 4 hours. So the game is pretty short. Also the game doesn’t have any extra game modes. The PC version is pretty barebones, as other systems had special game modes after completion. Luckily you do have some secret weapons and costumes to unlock. 

🎧Sound - The music in the game is incredible! It still ages like fine wine. The safe room theme is beautiful, along with many other soundtracks you hear around the mansion. The voice acting is as you expect. It’s corny, terrible, and iconic. Enemies and gun sounds do sound decent as well. Not much bad to say here. Besides the funny and terrible voice acting, everything in the sound department is good, especially those soundtracks.

❗Bugs❗- I haven’t encountered any bugs from my playthrough. So nothing here to write down.

🔅Performance - Performance is good. I had no issues. I mean it’s a super old game so I would expect it to run well lol. You should have no issues. I think any computer in the world can run this game no problem.

✔️Pro’s✔️
[list]
[*]Good enemy variety
[*]Great classic soundtracks
[*]Ammo and health conservation
[*]Amazing game setting and lore
[*]Two playable characters (Jill/Chris)
[*]Many puzzles and rooms to explore
[*]Secret unlockables (costumes & weapons)
[*]Controls feel good and no need for tweaking
[*]Able to play the very first RE game on Steam
[/list]

❌Con’s❌
[list]
[*]Only 30 FPS
[*]Unable to swap rounds in grenade launcher
[*]No extra game modes (other RE1 releases had them)
[*]No Steam overlay (fixable with a mod called RE: Enhanced)
[/list]
        
🏆Rating - 8/10
This game is easily worth the full price!

🔗Conclusion - Resident Evil was such a great experience. I’m so happy Capcom released this game on Steam. Being able to play this classic along with the RE: Enhanced mod really made the game a blast to go through. I’m excited to see how the other two classics are in this wonderful trilogy. This is easily a must buy, especially for fans of the franchise.

It was around this time 30 years ago that the term "SURVIVAL HORROR" was coined, and to accompy it, the first RESIDENT EVIL game was released. 

Originally pitched as a 3D remake of the Japan-exlusive Famicom adaptation of the 1989 horror film SWEET HOME, the original RESIDENT EVIL is a further evolution of both SWEET HOME and 1991's ALONE IN THE DARK, complete with tank controls, pre-rendered camera angles, limited inventory and the concept of careful management for your resources, otherwise you'd end up dead.

Following a series of murders in the Arklay Mountains, outside of the titular Raccoon City, S.T.A.R.S Bravo team went to invistigate, but following radio silence, Alpha team was later deployed, and came accross what remained of Bravo team, on top of monsters all over the place.

You take control of either Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield, and picking one or the other affects how you plan your trip throughout the mansion. Jill has 8 inventory slots, a lockpick but lesser health, while Chris only has 6(!) inventory slots and has to deal with more enemies, but can take a few more hits. Both characters have their own unique partner, with Barry "Jill Sandwich" Burton and rookie Bravo team medic Rebecca Chambers. 

For gameplay, I don't have to say much since this is RESIDENT EVIL we're talking about. Item management, space and careful planning of your routes is the name of the game here, along with being able to dodge enemies wherever possible. Though, Jill does have a much easier time compared to Chris, given that she has Barry to ensure that she gets the shotgun early and access to a grenade launcher, which makes quick work of certain enemies. Chris is more reliant on Rebecca to complete certain objectives as well. 

In terms of presentation, the live-action sequences are hilarious in a B-movie kind of way, while the voice acting is legendary for how hammy it is. Despite those, the atmosphere, tension and the music really sells the idea of the mansion being overrun by the undead and various bioweapons. The puzzles are all well thought out and are easy to understand once you get the hang of things.

Despite being 30 years old now, the original RESIDENT EVIL still plays really well, even against what is considered one of the greatest remakes of all time with the 2002 title (later remastered in 2015), and is a must-try for anyone wanting to experience the history of how survival horror got its start in gaming.

8/10.

Resident Evil, developed and published by CAPCOM Co., Ltd. and later distributed through platforms like GOG.com, stands as one of the most important and formative titles in video game history. It did not simply introduce players to a new franchise—it effectively defined what survival horror would become for years to follow. Built on a careful balance of tension, exploration, and resource management, the game creates an experience that feels deliberate and methodical, drawing players into a world where vulnerability is constant and every action must be considered.

Set within the eerie confines of the Spencer Mansion, the game casts players as either Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, members of a special task force investigating a string of brutal incidents. What begins as a straightforward mission quickly spirals into a nightmarish scenario involving biological experimentation and grotesque creatures. The story itself leans into familiar horror themes, but its strength lies in how it unfolds. Rather than overwhelming players with exposition, the game allows its narrative to emerge gradually through notes, environmental details, and carefully timed discoveries. This approach creates a sense of mystery that encourages curiosity while reinforcing the unsettling tone of the experience.

The gameplay is intentionally restrictive, and this is where much of its brilliance lies. Movement is slow and deliberate, combat is risky, and resources are scarce. Ammunition must be conserved, healing items are limited, and inventory space is tightly constrained. These elements force players to think strategically, often choosing avoidance over confrontation. The need to plan routes, manage items, and revisit areas creates a rhythm that is both tense and rewarding. While modern players may initially find these mechanics cumbersome, they are essential to the game’s identity, turning even simple encounters into moments of genuine suspense.

A defining aspect of the game is its presentation. The use of fixed camera angles and pre-rendered backgrounds gives each room a cinematic quality, allowing for carefully composed shots that heighten tension and obscure threats. The mansion itself feels alive, not in a literal sense but as a space filled with secrets, hidden pathways, and a lingering sense of dread. Sound design plays an equally critical role, with ambient noises, distant footsteps, and sudden audio cues working together to maintain a constant feeling of unease. The combination of visual and auditory elements creates an atmosphere that remains effective even decades later.

Of course, certain aspects of the game reflect its age. The voice acting, particularly in the opening sequences, is often remembered for its awkward delivery, and the live-action cutscenes can feel unintentionally campy. The control scheme, commonly referred to as “tank controls,” may also feel rigid compared to modern standards. However, these elements have become part of the game’s character, contributing to its distinct identity rather than detracting from it. In many ways, the slightly awkward presentation enhances the experience, adding an extra layer of unpredictability and discomfort.

From a historical standpoint, the impact of Resident Evil (1996) is immense. It established a framework that countless games would build upon, introducing mechanics and design principles that became synonymous with survival horror. The emphasis on limited resources, environmental storytelling, and atmospheric tension set a new standard for how fear could be conveyed in an interactive medium. Its success demonstrated that games could deliver not just thrills, but sustained psychological tension, influencing both its own sequels and an entire generation of developers.

What makes the game endure is not just its legacy, but the strength of its design. Even when stripped of nostalgia, it remains a tightly constructed experience that understands how to control pacing and maintain tension. It does not rely on constant action or spectacle; instead, it builds fear through anticipation, uncertainty, and careful design choices. This restraint is what gives the game its lasting power, allowing it to remain compelling long after its technical limitations have become apparent.

In the end, Resident Evil (1996) is more than just a starting point for a long-running series—it is a masterclass in atmosphere and design. Its influence can still be felt across the industry, and its core ideas continue to resonate with players who appreciate a slower, more deliberate approach to horror. While it may require patience to fully appreciate, those who invest the time will find an experience that is as tense and memorable today as it was at release.

I've owned 4 copies of this game, 4 different versions, since about 2001.  7 copies and versions if you include copies of the remake.  Overall, THIS is the best version (excluding the remake and aside from POSSIBLY the OG PS1, but that's only if you want the challenge).  (Actually, the PS1 version is prohibitively expensive anyway and too rare for all of us to have).

This is better than the PS5 director's cut digital version for at least a couple reasons:

1.  You can skip the door opening animations.
2.  The FMVs are MUCH better.  This is the PC version, so the gore is hilariously over the top.  Think Re-Animator, Evil Dead 2, Braindead/Dead Alive, etc.  The opening live action cinematic is in color, unlike the PS versions.  I do prefer the black and white actually, b/c it disguises the cartoonishness and the poor video quality.  HOWEVER, overall this version is better b/c it includes closeup footage of the victims instead of the grainy newspaper clippings of the PS versions, as well as closeups of the cerberus (dogs) tearing into the limbs of the STARS members and getting their faces literally shot off, with hilarious amounts of blood and gore flying around everywhere, all of which is cut out of the PS versions.  The live, atrocious actors are literally covered head to foot in blood and the laughs from this FMV alone are worth more than the $5 this version will cost you.  The 2nd cutscene includes a severed head dropping from the first zombie you encounter, which is also cut from the PS version.

This is better than the OG big box PC version b/c it's less choppy, controls better (or I just got better?), and looks better.  Also you don't need a box which takes up 60% of your apartment.  The steam version is about 4 GB if I remember correctly, so it's way bigger than the original PC version.  I left my OG big box back in PA a couple decades ago b/c it was just too big.

....As for comparison with the OG PS1 game.  There are still reasons to play that one over this.  I'm not saying that either version is objectively better, but the PS1 original is different enough that it's debatable.  There was NO auto aim in that one and it would sometimes take 7 shotgun shells to kill a hunter.  I recently replayed that version about a week ago and actually became low on ammo before the end of the game.  When I just played the PS5 digital director's cut a few days ago, I ended the game with an absurd amount of ammo for all weapons, the difficulty is a joke in comparison.  In this steam version, unfortunately it's possibly even easier b/c the range of the knife seems to be a lot longer.  The fact that you can slice zombies up more easily here than in the PS5 director's cut is no reason to pick the PS5 version over this though, b/c you never even need the knife in that version, that's how much ammo they give you.

Even if challenge is extremely important to you though, there's no reason not to pick this version up for $5.  The only arguably better version is the original PS1, and if you can justify spending over $100 for that, then there's no way you'll miss the $5 spent on this, for the opening 2 cutscenes alone.

I don't even regret the $10 I recently spent on the PS5 director's cut b/c there are slightly different unlockables and most importantly, my PS5 is hooked up to an 85" UHD Samsung, whereas this laptop isn't.  If you've got a PC hooked up to a badass tv though, no need for the PS5 version at all if you've got this.

As for how good the actual game is outside of comparing versions....  There are very few games I love enough to buy over and over again.  I don't plan on dying before I play the Sega Saturn version of this one.  One day, I'm gonna drop a few hundred for that experience.  It's a classic for a reason.

It is VERY nice to see the Original Classic Trilogy finally come to Steam. I really don't think RE1 1996 gets enough credit these days. It may not be the best entry in the Resident Evil franchise, but it was an extremely solid start and it helped popularize and shape the genre of survival horror.

Story:
The story, its characters, the dialogue, and the voice acting are all ♥♥♥♥. And that's why it's so iconic. It's one of those, “it's so bad, it's hilariously entertaining” type deals. I also give it a pass because games around this time were still trying to find their footing in story telling.

Resource & Inventory Management:
For a first entry, the gameplay is very solid. Enemies are threatening and ammo and healing is scarce. It's fun planning out the perfect amount of items to take with you while you create a route for the Mansion in your head and try to utilize your supplies as effectively as possible.

Enemy Selection:
Enemy selection is pretty alright. You've got your zombies, dogs, crows, and Chimeras, all requiring different methods to put them down, or avoid. Spiders are here too, but their inclusion is pretty weak considering they only appear in two rooms that are completely skippable. Other than that, the line up is good.

Hunters:
You may have noticed that I didn't mention Hunters though. They're a pain in the ass and seriously cause the quality of the game to take a hit in the last third. I-frames galore, rapid stunlocking, fast movement, AND a one hitter quitter, these guys just aren't fun to deal with in the slightest.

Bosses:
Bosses are pretty weak. Yawn is alright, Plant 42 is probably the best boss in the game since a lot of the player's choices can affect how the boss fight plays out, but the second Yawn fight is more of the same, Black Tiger is pathetic, and so are the two Tyrant fights. I'm not even sure if you can call Neptune a boss.

Choices:
There's a couple choices you're able to make throughout the game that'll actually affect certain events, determine the fate of certain characters, and give you a different ending. There's eight entire endings, each with different cutscenes. It's admittedly very impressive for the time.

Locations:
The layout of the Mansion is awesome. Rooms lead you through the Mansion and interconnect in an almost perfect way so that you can experiment a lot with the most optimal routing possible. Locations later on are a bit weaker since they’re much more linear and therefore have less opportunities for routing, but they're still a decent enough time.

Typewriters & Item Boxes:
The game does have some problems with typewriter and item box placements, two specifically, that being a missing item box at the start of the Tunnels, and a missing typewriter and item box at the start of the Labs. Not sure why these weren't included, but it makes both areas a hassle to get through on a first playthrough.

Tank Controls:
As you know, navigating this game requires you to use tank controls, and to put it bluntly, if you think tank controls are bad, you just suck at them lol. Coming from someone who's relatively new to the franchise, they work perfectly fine.

Puzzles:
Puzzles on the other hand aren't the best. They're okay. Mostly a lot of really simple “use this thing on that thing” stuff. There are a couple sliding box puzzles that are a slog but they're mostly few and far between.

Character Differences:
Finally, there's the character difference, which in practice, sort of works as a difficulty selection. Jill works great as an Easy playthrough, and Chris ramps up the difficulty perfectly for a player who has prior experience and knowledge through their first Jill playthrough. The glaring issue is that most players are more likely to play as Chris first, not knowing that Chris is the game's hard mode.

This happens for two reasons. First, the Japanese release of the game actually had Jill labeled as Easy, and Chris labeled as Hard. This was removed from Western releases and both the Director’s Cut and Dualshock Director's Cut. Alongside the difficulty indicators being removed in most releases, the character selection screen always hovers over Chris first. So if a Western player, or anyone who played DC or DS DC first, boots up the game and sees that Chris is automatically hovered over instead of Jill, chances are they'll assume the game wants them to play as Chris first and pick him.

This can really make or break whether or not your first experience with RE1 is a fun one, or a miserable one, because Chris’ playthrough is built with the idea of the player having prior experience with Jill's playthrough in mind. If the player doesn't have that experience because they pick Chris first, they're in for a very rough playthrough.

OST:
I really like most of the OST here. It gives off a very weird in an unsettling way vibe that I think really helps give this game a unique atmosphere which can't really be found in any other RE game.

Side Content:
I am a little bummed that we didn't somehow get a Director's Cut port for it's exclusive Advanced mode, but considering there's already a perfectly good PC port to throw onto Steam, I understand why they didn't pull an entirely brand new DC port out of their ass. Since this is a port of the Original PS1 release, there's not much here in terms of side content. You can unlock the secret closest key for bonus outfits by beating the game with the best ending, and if you beat the game in under three hours, you can unlock the infinite rocket launcher. A sub three hour run is super fun, as it really tests your inventory management, resource management, and routing skills. It's very satisfying to pull off.

Final Verdict:
While it has its obvious flaws, over time, I've found myself slowly coming to appreciate RE1 more and more. It went from a game that I thought was okay to a very solid first entry that is always fun to revisit, and that I'd actually rank above quite a few of the other mainline entries. I don't wanna give it too much credit, but I also don't wanna give it too little credit, so I think the rating here is a perfect middle ground.

First of all, I'm playing this on Linux, and as with an unfortunate amount of games on here, this one requires a little troubleshooting to fix. For anyone else on Linux, here's how I got it to work:

1) Install Protontricks and the latest ProtonGE if you haven't already.
2) Launch Protontrcks and then select Resident Evil, then select the default wineprefix
3) Then run regedit
4) Back on steam, click manage > browse local files and copy (not move!) the re1_english.reg to your desktop or documents
5) On Protontricks, click registry, then import registry file, then select the re1_english.reg you copied
6) Exit Protontricks and then right click Resident Evil and click properties
7) In launch options, paste this command: WINEDLLOVERRIDES="ddraw.dll=n,b" %command%
8) In compatibility, select ProtonGE

And that's what got it to work for me! Still has some issues but largely I've been playing it completely fine for the past 2 hours.

This is the uncensored release too, so if your only experience with this 1996 classic is the PlayStation or Saturn versions, then you'll get the full fat gory experience as intended; in colour too. Note that this is VANILLA RE1; no battle mode or arranged mode/dualshock soundtrack!

I recommend also maybe installing mods to alleviate these issues and to improve the pre-rendered backgrounds too. The voice acting is objectively terrible too, but there's an endearing charm to it in a David Lynch/Alfred Hitchcock kind of way, but maybe you won't see it like that and thats fine! I'm still going to give it a positive review, but a THIRTY YEAR OLD game does NOT need DRM in it.

So! This release is not great. For me, I own it and the other two classic RE games just to own them on Steam. If that's what you want, stop reading this review and just buy them for the library entries. 

But for a game to actually play? You're in for a bit of a mess without installing mods - and by installing mods, I mean deleting everything Steam downloads and dragging over the installation of a better version of RE1. 

Out of 1, 2 and 3 this is the second best port. Controls almost work perfectly out of the box... if you're willing to use only the joystick to move, anyway. I've got a little tip for classic RE games: Using the joystick sucks. Tank controls work best with a DPad, and the Xinput implementation here doesn't want to let you use the Dpad in bindings. 

Getting past that, it's the classic RE1 PC port experience. The game runs a little fast by default - not to the extent of an unpatched install of RE1PC, but this is still a game that wants to run as fast as your CPU will let it. 

And then you gotta look at it. This isn't really the fault of this port, these are pre-rendered backgrounds in a game that came out a year and a half or so in the PS1's life; they're low res 320x200 images and they're highly compressed. At modern resolutions you're gonna be seeing compression block artifacts as big as your hand. For someone who grew up with these games, I can look past it, but for someone who has never even smelled an RE game older than 4 it will probably be super distracting. 

But - it's still the PC port, and that means you have a couple of cool features. Beating the game will get you some unlockable machine guns which no other version of RE1 has. You can skip door loading scenes, and the intro is uncut and in full color. Jill has unlimited saves on her first playthrough and Chris...

Well, Chris is still hardmode. 

Also, weird DRM, strange choice for games that were already re-released on GOG and for this one in particular which is 30 years old.

But I love Resident Evil. I want Capcom to know I still love these old games to death and will crawl through broken glass to play them. But I can't recommend purchasing them unless you've got the same classic RE brainrot. There are better ways to play this classic game.
